text: Welcome to AI and Agentic Automation with Power Automate. You already know how to call a model. What you're about to learn is the layer around that call — when it fires, what feeds it, and where the result goes next. That's orchestration, and this chapter is a fast, essentials-only pass aimed at engineers, not the full platform course.

If you've built anything with an LLM API, you've already written orchestration code by hand. A script that polls an inbox, calls a model, and writes a result is an orchestration pipeline. Power Automate is a managed runtime for exactly that: triggers instead of polling loops, actions instead of SDK calls, and a connector catalog instead of writing an auth flow for every system you touch.

The problem this actually solves isn't the model call — it's reliability. Every flow run gets logged with its full input and output. A failed HTTP call can retry automatically. And you can require a named person to approve a step before anything irreversible happens. That's the same infrastructure Power Automate offered before AI Builder existed, which is exactly why it's a sensible place to put the plumbing.

You won't replace your model code with this — you'll wrap it. Power Automate runs on the same underlying engine as Azure Logic Apps, so retries and run-after settings carry over almost exactly. And throughout this course, every example uses Castlebridge Logistics, a fictional regional trucking and warehousing company connecting its AI projects to email, SharePoint, and its dispatch database.
Hold onto that frame — Power Automate is the connective tissue around your AI calls, not a replacement for them. Up next, lesson two: flows, triggers, and actions, the essentials.
